Having thus recited the great mantra of the Vajra-samādhi of all phenomena, one performs various offerings according to the methods of the Padma-kula; whatever is performed will be accomplished.
Furthermore, he spoke on the method for accomplishing all ritual procedures and images of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha:

"Within the image, one should draw a great solar disc according to the rite; within the disc, one should draw the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, whose body is the color of lapis lazuli, seated upon a lotus flower of various colors."
On each side of the bodhisattva atop that flower, one should paint four attendant bodhisattvas, namely:
the Bodhisattva Abhiṣeka, the Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha, the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, and the Bodhisattva Mahāpūjā.
Once this has been painted, it immediately becomes the supreme maṇḍala.

This subtle vajra, the Great Sun-Disk that Universally Illuminates, the Tathāgata Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva, perfectly fulfills all vows; he is the secret bell of the Dharma-jewel, who skillfully bestows all desires. All supreme accomplishments of the ultimate aspirations and so forth are attained through this method, whereby one obtains the sublime bliss of liberation and fulfills all intentions.
Whether performed by oneself or for another, this supreme samādhi is entirely perfected; by means of this dharma, one can swiftly accomplish Vajrasattva.
"Because this dharma is the most supreme among all ritual manuals for accomplishment.
He further spoke the ritual manual for the samādhi of the supreme great mudrā of Sarvārthasiddhivajrasattva:

"If there are sentient beings of inferior faculties who have committed various sinful karmas and performed non-beneficial actions, upon seeing this dharma, their sinful karmas will be extinguished; they shall become great bodhisattvas and, through great skillful means, be able to benefit sentient beings."
Just as Vajrasattva abides in the firm and true three karmas, not transgressing samādhi and dwelling securely within the Vajradhātu, one should thereafter transmit the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā).
Having received the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), one attains all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Regarding this method of the Great Seal, even the Buddhas themselves do not dare to transgress its samādhi.

Those who seek Vajrasattva or even those who seek to attain Buddhahood cannot achieve it even after the passage of ten million eons (*koṭi-kalpa*); yet, by the power of this supreme Great Seal, one can swiftly attain accomplishment as a Buddha or Bodhisattva and, according to the various inclinations of the sentient beings to be converted, shall explain the methods for their respective accomplishments.
This Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is a great skillful means, for it is well able to bring all phenomena to perfect fulfillment. Why is this so?
When this Great Seal is bound, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas gather like clouds and, in a single instant, bestow whatever is desired.
Having performed the offering in this manner, he further praised it, saying:

"Vajrasattva is the most supreme skillful means, subtle, profound, vast, pure, and of the nature of non-existence; inexhaustible and unending, he is the ultimate pinnacle. He gives rise to the great bliss and joy that pervades the entire realm of empty space; he is definitively unfailing in bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment, and his supreme accomplishment is that of Great Sovereignty."

By means of subtle and wondrous syllables, they give rise to all meanings; by means of the vajra awakening of the Dharma, they cause all sentient beings to realize supreme great bliss; and by means of the vajra secret implements, they cause all sentient beings to abide in the foremost Dharma.
Then he spoke the ritual for the supreme secret accomplishment of the samādhi of all Tathāgatas:
"The practitioner, always at the time of early dawn, should bind the great mudrā according to the rite and recite the heart-mantra; thus one immediately achieves accomplishment in all mudrās."
"Furthermore, regarding the supreme secret method of accomplishment:
the practitioner, in accordance with the ritual, should hold the vajra bell and scepter and recite the three kinds of samaya-mantras; thus, all sought-after accomplishments will be fully realized."

Furthermore, if one holds the vajra and bell according to the ritual and binds the Viśva-mudrā while reciting the mantra, one will immediately attain the accomplishment of all mudrās, and one’s body will become like that of Vajrasattva.

All the methods for achieving great mastery shall be bestowed upon them; the various mudrās will swiftly reach perfection, and even all methods of accomplishment will be achieved, such that there is nothing that will not be fulfilled according to their wishes.
Furthermore, he spoke this Dharma-gate of the ritual procedures for the supreme secret of all correspondences:
"What is called 'correspondence' refers to the function of all phenomena, because all realms are produced from the dharma of correspondence."
How is it produced?
It is because it is produced from the right mindfulness of the deity.
Furthermore, what is meant by "correspondence" (*yoga*)?
This refers precisely to speech.
The essence of speech is sound, and sound is the principle of the great correspondence (*mahā-yoga*).
The principle of correspondence is the right mindfulness of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity); through this correspondence, one is born as that very *iṣṭadevatā*.
Because it is born from the *iṣṭadevatā*, it is called the accomplishment of union (*yoga-siddhi*).
Furthermore, this "union" refers to the union of gathering, the union of all mudrās and dharmas, and so forth.
Regarding "correspondence through aggregation," it refers to the coming together of various dharmas; this is called correspondence through aggregation.
For example, just as there is an accumulation of much wealth in the world, so too is the coming together of various dharmas.
The gathering of all seal-dharmas (*mudrā-dharma*), samādhis, and so forth, is called "gathering-correspondence" (*saṃgraha-yoga*).
Furthermore, regarding the correspondence of all seal-dharmas: it refers to the essence and characteristics of the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is termed "all seal-dharmas."
This application is the supreme accomplishment itself.
That is to say, because one should employ each of the fundamental mudrās belonging to all the noble ones (ārya), from these arise the most secret accomplishment of the Great Yoga method.

The practitioner should contemplate in accordance with the mudrā method of the deity; next, they should imagine their own body to be likewise, for by doing so, they will immediately attain the perfect realization of the stages of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. This ritual for the most supreme secret accomplishment is a profound and unsurpassed method of attainment; one should, in accordance with the deity, grasp the Great Viśva-mudrā.
The practitioner should contemplate their own body in this same way, and thus achieve the formation of the subtle and wondrous syllable.
This is the most supreme among all dharmas; it is the highest correspondence with the Great Viśva-samādhi, which encompasses all dharmas of joy and bliss.

Furthermore, within this ritual procedure for the supreme secret accomplishment, the method for the supreme accomplishment should be in accordance with the fundamental correspondence of Vajrasattva, both in essence and in form.

The practitioner should imagine their own body in this same way, thereby attaining the subtle and wondrous meaning of the syllables. From this, they obtain the pure samādhi of all Buddhas and immediately become the master of all correspondences. Among all accomplishments, such a method of correspondence is supreme; there is nothing that can be undertaken which will not be achieved.

Even when experiencing the pleasures of the five desires, one should simply contemplate them as being in union with the *iṣṭadevatā* (the chosen deity). This is the supreme secret, unsurpassed Great Vehicle, and pure Great Samādhi of all Tathāgatas; it is the fundamental union of the Great Bliss of all Tathāgatas, which is the Vajra-Definitive Samādhi.
This yoga is a supreme medicine, for it possesses the most excellent efficacy; it is that which grants mastery over all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

The practitioner should know that if one cultivates this yoga, one will immediately attain the vigor and bliss of Vajrasattva, and be able to increase physical strength, vitality, and lifespan. All ritual methods for accomplishment will be fully perfected in a single instant.

Why is this? Because by practicing such a corresponding Great Seal (mahāmudrā) and abiding in such a correspondence, one performs the rites for the accomplishment of the samādhi of correspondence in accordance with the ritual for the accomplishment of the deity's correspondence.

Furthermore, the practitioner should know that the mind is like a magical illusion, having no fixed abode; the body is like a vessel formed through fabrication. The body is not conscious, for it is neither separate from the mind nor not separate from it.
The application of this seal-method is likewise so.
For example, because the phenomena of form and mind are fundamentally not one, the body and mind unite to perform all manner of activities.
The same applies to the union of the mudrā and the dharma.
Thus, this samādhi and its corresponding [practices] mutually bring about accomplishment.
If practitioners cultivate various accomplishments through the yoga of the dharma of non-self, these practitioners are themselves the Tathāgata.

"Furthermore, regarding all that is associated with mudrās: it means that the essence of the mudrā is endowed with great bliss and firmness; by virtue of this great bliss and firmness, one accomplishes all matters associated with bliss."

If any practitioners diligently seek this supreme secret method of accomplishment, they should simply apply themselves with vigor, generating the bodhicitta and maintaining focused, dedicated effort. They must not exhaust themselves through arduous ascetic practices that lead to weariness and subsequent regression; rather, they should accomplish the practice with a joyful mind in resonance with great bliss. This is called the method of union with all mudrās.
Furthermore, those who are associated with bliss are able to accomplish the rites of siddhi.
This is because they experience all dharmas of bliss as appropriate, according to the dharma of great bliss associated with the *iṣṭadevatā*.
This is the supreme secret, unsurpassed Mahāyāna King of Great Teachings of all Tathāgatas, for it is the method of the supreme great bliss corresponding with Vajrasattva.
"Furthermore, 'conjoined with all that is pleasant' means being accomplished through conjunction with all samādhis.
A practitioner who cultivates this dharma should be conjoined with a pleasant mind."

Why is this? If one applies oneself with strenuous effort, it will produce distress within one's own being; consequently, one will become distracted regarding the Dharma and will be unable to focus single-mindedly to accomplish the various attainments.

Therefore, one who practices the yoga of cultivation may enjoy food and drink according to their inclination and capacity; even in the four modes of deportment, including laughter and speech, they will encounter no further hindrance in any situation.

Even those who have not entered the maṇḍala or who possess various obstacles and afflictions, if they practice the sādhana of accomplishment in accordance with the yoga of their chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), will, in a single instant, all become fully perfected as the Sovereign of Samādhi of Great Desire and Bliss, the King of the Vajra Families.

If one seeks to realize the state of all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas, even by means of this corresponding practice (*yoga*), accomplishment is attained; how much more so for those who seek various mundane accomplishments?

This method of definitive accomplishment brings success in all things; it can perfect all secret mudrās and bring an end to the limits of suffering. Because this correspondence is so subtle and wondrous, it is called the supreme method of delight of Vajrasattva.

Furthermore, "all that is associated with firmness" means that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is firm; from the beginning to the end, it is solely true wisdom, for its firm intrinsic nature has no distinct essence.

Furthermore, regarding "the correspondence with the firm prophecy": this refers to relying on the skillful means of the great wisdom of the deity-correspondence (*devatā-yoga*) to bring to definitive fulfillment all matters sought through the rites for accomplishment; this is called the correspondence with the firm prophecy.

Furthermore, that which corresponds to the supreme secret, firm prophecy is the Great Corresponding Rite of Vajrasattva; by performing various offerings, one attains the fulfillment of all diverse aims, and this is called the correspondence of prophecy.
Then he spoke in verse:
“This truth is supreme; it is the subtle and wondrous Dharma of correspondence.
Within the most profound secrets, it is the most honored, victorious, and peerless.”
If a great ācārya and a disciple of superior intelligence possess the great bodhicitta,
they may transmit this yoga-dharma. However,
if they encounter one who lacks wisdom, even if that person desires accomplishment, [it should not be given].
Do not transmit this to one who lacks faith and understanding in the Dharma.
This Dharma is not difficult to accomplish; it does not require arduous ascetic practices.
By merely following the ritual procedures, one will successfully achieve accomplishment.
One who arouses diligence in their practice attains great benefit;
liberated from all demonic activities, they cannot be seen even by the gods.
This is Vajrasattva, who has realized the path of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"This supreme yoga shall all be brought to complete fulfillment.
Thus ends the sixth fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-paramādya-mūla-sukha-vajra-amogha-samaya-mahātantrarāja*.

Chapter Twenty-Four: The Section on the Mudrās of Supreme Accomplishment. At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi proclaimed this definitive, non-empty, supreme, skillful, subtle, vast, inconceivable, and profoundly deep Dharma, through which all methods of accomplishment—whether finite or infinite—are entirely able to be realized:

"The practitioner should, according to their inclination and wherever they may be, sit in the full lotus posture with a mind made supple and gentle. Then, with the left hand, they should form the firm seal of Sarvajñatā (All-Knowledge) and place it beside the left hip; with the right hand, they should playfully brandish the vajra. Because of the accomplishment of the three vajra-actions, this is Vajrasattva."

By relying on such ritual procedures, one swiftly achieves stability and non-retrogression, reaching even the stages of the great Bodhisattvas and the Tathāgatas, attaining great mastery over all accomplishments; thus, Vajrasattva is firm in all respects.

Furthermore, if a practitioner who has not yet entered a maṇḍala cultivates this Great Seal (mahāmudrā), they will receive the respect and offerings of all Buddhas, obtain all noble riches, and attain mastery over great bliss.
This great secret mudrā is the most supreme within the three realms; by accomplishing this great mudrā, one becomes no different from Vajrasattva himself.
All accomplishments, various activities, and the great sublime bliss—all these are fully perfected through this great mudrā, such that there is no sought-after dharma that is not accomplished.
Furthermore, he spoke of the Fundamental Great Seal of Vajrasattva:

"By means of this seal, within all maṇḍalas, all various methods of accomplishment—such as summoning through samaya-hooks, causing entry, awakening, and inspiring love—are brought to fulfillment; it is also called the Vajra Secret Samaya Seal."
The mudrā in which the ten fingers are joined together is called the Vajra-joined palms; furthermore, when the ten fingers are interlaced like a fist, it is called the Vajra-bind.

With this vajra-bind, extend the two index fingers and the two thumbs; then bend the two middle fingers into the palms and join them with the two thumbs. The two index fingers should be held straight and level like a vajra. This is called the fundamental great seal of Vajrasattva; it is this very fundamental great seal.
Furthermore, with the two middle fingers curved like hooks and placed at the heart as if performing the gesture of summoning, this is called the Vajrāṅkuśa-mudrā (Vajra Hook Seal).
This Vajrāṅkuśa-mudrā brings about great amorous delight with Vajrasattva.

If one employs this hook mudrā and heart mantra for the purpose of summoning, Vajrasattva will give rise to great love and respect, swiftly descend into the maṇḍala, and one shall attain the great desire and great bliss of Vajrasattva.

Having thus summoned them, all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, as well as all sentient beings, shall be equally and swiftly summoned; if any who are summoned do not descend, they shall be swiftly destroyed.
Furthermore, he taught the *argha* mudrā of the Great Bliss Vajra Samādhi Heart:

"First, one should form with both hands the gesture resembling a vajra bowl; then, bind the aforementioned Vajra Mudrā; finally, with the two middle fingers like flower branches, one should empower it with the heart mantra."
If one bestows empowerment by means of this Samādhi Arghya Mudrā, that person shall attain all sovereign powers.
The efficacy of this mudrā is also like that of the preceding mudrā; it may be employed for all dharmas.
Furthermore, the mudrā of the banner for entering the maṇḍala is taught:

"One should hold three fingers upright with the right hand like a banner, join the tips of the thumb and the little finger, and perform playful dancing and singing; then, having entered the maṇḍala, one first prostrates to the principal deity."
If one binds this mudrā and enters the maṇḍala, one immediately becomes a Vajrācārya and will certainly accomplish the rites of offering.
Thereafter, according to one's capacity and inclination, one should present offerings such as incense, flowers, and insignia.
Furthermore, using the banner-binding mudrā, prostrate to the *iṣṭadevatā* (chosen deity) and utter these words:
"I now prostrate to the *iṣṭadevatā*.
Having spoken thus, immediately perform the vajra-palms-joined gesture and place it upon the crown of the head; prostrate to Vajrasattva and all the Tathāgatas, and offer praise.
Then, with both hands, form the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*), interlace the thumbs, and bend the index fingers, placing them upon one's own crown like a jeweled tiara.
Next, changing to the vajra-fist, form the gesture of binding a garland on the left and right sides of the crown, and then again assume the posture of hanging ribbons.

Having performed this seal-rite, one should visualize that Vajrasattva bestows empowerment upon oneself; thereafter, one should personally sprinkle the crown of one's head with the nectar-water of Great Bliss-Vajra.
Once the consecration has been performed, all the dharmas of a Vajrācārya will be accomplished.

Furthermore, if one is to bestow the consecration upon a disciple, one should perform the *vajra-añjali* mudrā as the *namaskāra-mudrā* and confer the consecration by presenting various exquisite flowers.

Thus, through these mudrā methods and the rituals of the various maṇḍalas, one immediately attains mastery over all accomplishments; this is called the ritual for the accomplishment of the Vajrasattva Mudrā.
Furthermore, the seal-method is taught:

"If one wishes to summon Vajrasattva, the practitioner should sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), bind the Great Bliss Secret Vajra Hook Seal (mahāsukha-guhyavajrāṅkuśamudrā), and recite the heart-mantra while performing the summoning. Thereafter, according to the ritual, one should present various offerings such as song and dance and offer praise. Again, binding the Playful Seal (līlāmudrā), one should prostrate and recite; because of these offerings of vajra song, dance, and so forth, the rites performed will immediately attain accomplishment."
Then he spoke this supreme secret Vajra Song:

“*Sarva-nuraga-sukha-svabhāva-nātha svāhā |* *Tvaṃ vajrasattva-parama-saurata |* *Bhava me mahāsukha-nercchaya-sarvārthada |* *Pratipadyasva jinagarbha-praṇata* If one constantly chants this Vajra Song, one will attain the firm love and respect of the Lord of Great Bliss (*Mahāsukha*) and accomplish all siddhis.”

This great secret song is to be constantly maintained within the fundamental mind. When offering praise, one should keep the lips and teeth joined; following the various ritual procedures, one does not depart from vajra speech and successfully accomplishes the dharmas of all families. Chanting songs such as the syllable *HŪṂ*, one acts according to one's capacity and desire, producing a subtle sound with well-regulated vocal activity to melodiously sing the dharma of Vajrasattva.

This song of supreme accomplishment should be recited at will in all places. One should employ the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Vajrasattva: with this seal, the left hand forms the wisdom-fist (*jñānamuṣṭi*) and the right hand holds a vajra. By means of this seal and its mantra, one should perform the rite of accomplishment.
"By means of these mudrās, all rites performed in reliance upon the *sādhana* of the respective deities and the application of the heart-mantras shall be accomplished.
He further explained the characteristics of the mudrās of all Tathāgatas:

"For these mudrās, one first forms the Vajrajñānamuṣṭi of all Tathāgatas with both hands; then, according to the rite of the Vajraratna-abhiṣeka, one performs the consecration by sprinkling [water] upon the five places."

Again, form the palms joined in the gesture of making an offering; then open the hands and form two fists. With the left fist facing outward, extend the index finger vertically; with the right fist facing inward, place it at the heart to form the mudrā. This is the Great Mudrā of the Wisdom Fist of all Tathāgatas, which is definitively unfailing.

When one binds this seal, one attains the stage of non-retrogression and shall realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This person cannot be seen; they are far removed from all fetters and restraints, and even the armies of Māra cannot disturb them.
Furthermore, one who binds this mudrā should regard it as being like the Buddha; if one makes offerings to such a person, it is equivalent to making offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Such is the ritual for this Great Seal (mahāmudrā); all samaya-mudrās, lotus-mudrās, and vajra-mudrās are likewise to be understood in this way.

Regarding what is called the *karmamudrā*: first, with both hands palms upturned, extend the two thumbs toward the index fingers and place them at the heart; then, form the seal as for the Jewel Consecration (*ratnābhiṣeka*).

Furthermore, as before, with both hands palms facing upward and each index finger slightly bent at the first joint, join the two middle fingers together like a vajra-lotus; this constitutes the Dharma-mudrā.
He then spoke this seal-mantra:

"Āḥ hūṃ hrīḥ hūṃ. Furthermore, one modifies the karma-mudrā by forming a vajra-fist with the left hand and bending the thumb inside the fist; this constitutes the Great Seal of the Wisdom Fist of all Tathāgatas.

"Furthermore, with the right hand, as if grasping the corner of a robe, hook it at the heart; then extend the hand to form the earth-touching gesture. This constitutes the mudrā for subduing all the hosts of Māra."

Furthermore, without altering this seal, one again forms the seal by turning the palms upward; this is called the Seal of Emergence, also called the Seal of Bestowing Boons, and also called the Seal of Prediction.

Furthermore, using this seal to grasp the corners of one's robe in the manner of opening a lotus flower constitutes the mudrā; it is named the "Seal for Producing Dharmas" and is also named the "Seal for Purifying All Dharmas."
Furthermore, with this same mudrā, extend three fingers upright like a banner; this constitutes the Banner Mudrā.
When this mudrā is bound, all prayers and aspirations will certainly be accomplished.
Furthermore, he taught the accomplishment of the Great Karma Seal of the Wisdom Fist of all Tathāgatas:
"If this seal is applied to the body of a sick person, that illness will be cured immediately."
"If it is settled within the mind, all poisons will be eliminated, and even the rites of false mudrās and mantras will all be destroyed.
He then explained:
"Oṃ hūṃ. "Using this mantra together with the aforementioned *karmamudrā* rite, its power will be accomplished."

If one forms the mudrās and recites this vidyā while rotating it around the body, one will attain great eloquence, and all the supreme, most secret mudrās of all Tathāgatas will become firmly established.

Thus, if one settles [the mind] within the sense faculties, one attains the perfection of those faculties; if, after recollecting the Buddhas, one rotates through the directions and returns the mind to its original state, whether seeking accomplishment for oneself or acting for the sake of others, one will in all cases attain great joy and bliss, even unto the realization of the Buddha’s Bodhi.

If one binds this mudrā and visualizes all the Buddhas, one should realize that the five aggregates are like a potter’s wheel; thereafter, with body prostrating in reverence, mouth reciting the great mantra, and mind maintaining right mindfulness and visualization, one abides in equanimity, mindfulness, ethical discipline, diligence, loving-kindness, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the power of skillful means. Thus, one firmly gives rise to the gateways of dhāraṇī, fulfills the ten stages, practices the four unhindered knowledges, and understands the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. By means of the Viśvakarman rite, one extensively benefits sentient beings, performing great Buddha-activities through the three vajra-actions.
Then he spoke these great vidyās: "Oṃ bodhicittavajri. "Oṃ samantabhadra-carī. "Oṃ jina..."

It produces subtle and wondrous sounds and possesses subtle and wondrous meanings; it is the great Dharma discourse, the heart-mind of all Buddhas, and is capable of definitively accomplishing all undertakings.
Having recited the names of all the Buddhas according to the Dharma, one should then achieve accomplishment through the right mindfulness of all Tathāgatas and the seals (mudrās) of all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, the mudrā-form of the Vajra Flame Solar Disc is explained as follows:

"First, bind the Great Vajra Mudrā; next, transform it into the Samaya Mudrā; thereafter, having formed the Vajra-bond, all fingers are like wheels of flame, and the two middle fingers form the seal like a vajra."
This mudrā can subdue the three realms and can also effect the rite of magnetizing for Vajrasattva.

Furthermore, without altering the previous mudrā, form a fist with the left hand and extend the index finger upward in the manner of a nail; with the right hand, form the mudrā like a hook. This is called the Mudrā of Subduing the Three Realms.
This mudrā is able to summon all.
Furthermore, having formed the wrathful fists with both hands, one then forms the *vajrāṅkuśa* (vajra-hook) in the manner of striking at the appointed time; this is called the Vajrāṅkuśa Mudrā.
This mudrā effectively accomplishes all tasks and is able to bring about all siddhis.
Furthermore, forming the vajra-joined palms with the ten fingers arranged like flames constitutes this mudrā; it is called the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī.
This mudrā effectively accomplishes various tasks and skillfully subdues all evils.
Furthermore, form the vajra-joined palms, then form the mudrā with the left hand in the gesture of a hook.
This mudrā can summon all things and can also perform the rites of entry and awakening; all shall be accomplished.
Furthermore, form a vajra-fist with the left hand, and form the mudrā with the right hand like a trident.
This mudrā can liberate one from all shackles, fetters, and bonds.
Furthermore, with both hands formed into the mudrā like a blossoming lotus,
this mudrā can sever all afflictions.
"Furthermore, with both hands forming the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*), the two thumbs joined together constitute this mudrā; it is also called the 'Mudrā for Subduing the Three Realms.
This mudrā is excellent for performing the supreme accomplishment of summoning and subjugation."
Furthermore, hooking the index finger of the right hand with the index finger of the left hand in the manner of drawing a bow constitutes this mudrā.
This mudrā is excellent for summoning and can also effect all forms of attraction.
Furthermore, as for the Seal of Subduing the Three Realms: form a vajra-fist with the right hand and extend the arm, placing the little finger against the back of the left hand to form the seal.
This seal effectively destroys all evil and heterodox seals and effectively accomplishes all siddhis.
Furthermore, with both hands forming the vajra-bind (vajrabandha), held supple yet firm, this constitutes the mudrā;
it is called the Vajrasiddhi-mudrā.
Furthermore, with both hands forming the vajra-bind, the two thumbs and index fingers are joined like a vajra-club (vajra-śūla) to form the mudrā.
This mudrā can destroy all evils.
All banner mudrās and bell mudrās constitute the most supreme dharmas; they too can destroy all evils and are preeminent within the three realms. This is the consecration mudrā of Vajrasattva.
Furthermore, regarding the mudrās of the noble ones of the Vajra Family: with both hands, one forms the vajra-fist.

According to this ritual procedure, the noble ones of the respective family are consecrated with the vajra-jewel; one performs the vajra-palms gesture, covers the face with a pure cloth, and positions the two thumbs like vajras.

Having performed the vajra initiation, one should then prostrate according to the ritual rules and take up the vajra. Thereupon, one should offer worship to the ācārya according to one's ability; thus, one will attain the accomplishment of all dharmas.
"These mudrās of the various families, when all bound according to the ritual and employed with the great mantras, will immediately bring about the accomplishment of one's activities.

together with one voice and different mouths, [spoke thus]:"

Thus, these secrets, the supreme and true principle,
were extensively taught as above for the sake of accomplishing the subtle syllables and for the broad benefit of sentient beings.
Having received the exhortation of all Buddhas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
he spoke the aforementioned Dharma:
"That which is called 'ritual procedure' refers to the ritual procedures of all dharmas."
This is a dharma that is without ritual procedure,
yet it manifests all ritual procedures; by means of such ritual procedures,
all dharmas are purified.
As for what is called the "Supreme Teaching," it refers to that which encompasses all phenomena and gives birth to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; this secret,
true principle is named the Supreme Teaching.
That which is called the "Root" refers to the wisdom of reality itself,
which pervades the realm of empty space and is as firm and solid as a vajra.
It is the Great Desire and Great Bliss, the most supreme and subtle syllable.
He is Vajrasattva, the true reality of all ritual manuals.
That which is said to be "originally non-existent" is like the intrinsic nature of space;
he is called Vajrasattva, the great adamantine body.
This is called primordial non-existence;
it is Great Sovereignty itself, which skillfully bestows all accomplishments.
It is the Lord of the Vajra Family, who delights in the subtle and wondrous syllables.
That which is called "great desire" refers to being free from all faults and thoroughly realizing the ultimate Dharma; this is what is meant by "great desire.
That which is called "great bliss" refers to the true and wondrous principle.
He is indeed Vajrasattva, for he is the source from which all things arise.
That which is called "the Good and Wise" refers to the pure Dharmadhātu;
it is the liberation of all Tathāgatas, pervading the body of Samantabhadra.
As for the "raised" posture (*utkṣipta-mudrā*), it refers to all accomplishments;
it is the supreme mudrā of mastery that summons all siddhis—
this is called the raised posture.
That which is called "among all dharmas," The sovereign Vajrapāṇi,
refers to the root teaching, The true and subtle principle.
If one recites and maintains it with a sincere heart, One shall obtain all merits.
This is called the Sovereign Vajrapāṇi among all phenomena;
that which is termed bodhicitta is the inconceivable,
vast, and profound Dharma that accomplishes all sublime bliss.
Capable of manifesting all transformations,
the pure bodhicitta thereby becomes firm; performing various sublime deeds,
one dwells in samādhi.
Born from Vajra Wisdom, produced from the Vajra,
he is named Vajrasattva; this is the body of all Buddhas,
and it is called the Bodhicitta.
That which is called "Great Vajra" refers to gathering all sentient beings and causing them to practice my teachings;
if one constantly cultivates the secret, true principle, one immediately becomes a Great Vajra.
What is called the practice of enlightenment (bodhicaryā) refers to observing that sentient beings are stained by and attached to various afflictions; for the sake of benefiting them,
one constantly practices the conduct of Samantabhadra— this is named the practice of enlightenment.
What is called "subduing Māra" refers to the very minds of all Māras;
this mind is itself the Tathāgata. If one can subdue this mind, there will be no further harassment by Māras;
this is what it means to conquer the armies of Māra.
What is called "realizing bodhi" means awakening to one's original mind and making firm the wisdom of bodhi;
by comprehending the true and wondrous principle,
one immediately achieves equal and perfect enlightenment— this is termed "realizing bodhi."
Furthermore, it is said that Vajrapāṇi subdues all evils and causes those who are deluded to attain awakening.
He is the firm resolve for bodhicitta, entrusted by all the Buddhas.
This is the truth of the Dharma-realm; by upholding it as one's weapon, one accomplishes all dharmas—thus he is named Vajrapāṇi.
What is called "born from the family" refers to Prajñāpāramitā as the mother.
Skillful means is understood as the father;
from the Vajra-hand gesture, the dharmas of all families are produced—this is called "birth from one's own family.
That which is called "desiring liberation" refers to great desire and great bliss.
One well attains all accomplishments; the phrases of the bliss of all accomplishments are themselves the Dharma of Great Bliss—this is called liberation through desire.
What are called the three types of names refer to the boundless [beings] of the three times.
He is able to subdue all beings and acts as the lord of the three realms;
he is further named the Three Jewels, and further named the Three Realms.
He is able to bring about all formations and destructions—these are his three names.
Regarding that which is called "everywhere," it is the Great Vajra of Great Bliss;
that is to say, for the sake of bringing vast benefit to all sentient beings,
his mind knows no fixed rest.
Abiding in a firm mind, thoroughly realizing the true meaning—
this is called "everywhere.
As for what is called the root song, as well as the inner and outer heart-mantras:
That which is called the most supreme among the three realms of existence, the accomplishment of great mastery;
the Bodhisattva’s benefit for sentient beings is this great desire and great bliss,
the secret and subtle phrase, the heart-mantra sung as the syllable HŪṂ.
Even up to the external heart-mantras, all are the wisdom of true reality.
Because one generates joy through the external secret mind, all that is performed is accomplished;
these are called the Root Songs and so forth.
That Amoghasamādhi is said to be the method for performing accomplishment;
through subtle and great bliss, whatever is performed attains accomplishment.
It is not obtained through arduous toil—this is the dharma of the Great Samādhi.
That which no Buddhas can transcend is called the "Non-empty Samādhi.
Regarding the eight maṇḍalas: according to their respective locations, one should simply employ their corresponding powers, each in accordance with the faculties and natures of those [beings].
Performing all dharmas according to the occasion, one immediately manifests the assembly of worthies and sages;
as for the retribution obtained thereby, one attains the merit of great ultimate realization.
Having constructed this maṇḍala, first observe the ten directions.
One should begin from the north and then stretch four lines,
arranging the forms of the eight altars all according to the fundamental ritual procedures.
In accordance with the correspondence to the *iṣṭadevatā*, one should visualize the completion of the maṇḍala.
The performance of all methods of accomplishment is precisely this maṇḍala;
it is the great principle of ultimate reality.
That which is called the "great secret" refers to all the secret dharmas.
Yet fundamentally nothing exists; this is the Great Bliss Vajra,
identical to the body of Samantabhadra, the great sovereign of the vajra hosts—
this is called the Great Secret.
What is called the deity’s practice refers to the fundamental and most supreme lord of the maṇḍala;
he is the highest great desire and the greatly joyful mind, ever manifesting a smiling countenance.
His body is like the color of the moon, adorned with various jewels;
his radiant light shines everywhere. He is the most supreme among those in the three realms of existence, bestowing upon all the realm of wondrous bliss;
he has perfectly accomplished subtle and sublime verses.
Therefore, it is designated as the *iṣṭadevatā*.
As for the principle of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), it refers to the merit of the Buddha-jewel, a dharma peerless within the three realms; this jewel alone is most supreme.
Those who receive the Buddha’s empowerment realize the rank of Dharma King;
this is called the principle of empowerment.
Regarding what is termed samādhi: one should sit in the full lotus posture.
Then, forming the seal of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*), press the left hand over the right;
visualize Vajrapāṇi—this is called *samādhi*.
As for the "assembly of noble ones" mentioned, it refers to the noble ones of the Vajra family.
This is the wisdom of ultimate reality, which thoroughly understands all things.
It is the most supreme of all accomplishments and the source of all great auspiciousness.
Possessing the noble wealth of all dharmas, it is the foremost among all phenomena.
All methods of accomplishment are the seals and signs of the noble ones;
they are Vajrasattva, the secret great sovereign.
What are called the five secrets refer to Vairocana.
As well as Akṣobhya Tathāgata, Ratnasaṃbhava,
Amitāyus, Amoghasiddhi, and so forth— these are called the five secrets.
As for what is termed the "families" (kulas), it refers to all the Tathāgatas.
Through the sublime principle of reality, one becomes Vajrasattva.
[One becomes] the Buddha Vairocana, the family of Akṣobhya Tathāgata,
Ratnasambhava, Amitāyus, Amoghasiddhi, and so forth.
Truth is likewise so.
One who skillfully subdues all evils uses purely wholesome means to shine universally, like the sun.
Benefiting all sentient beings and perfectly accomplishing all teachings,
the Viśvakarma-vajra family is the great means of gathering [beings].
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara relies upon the Lotus family.
One attains the supreme siddhi;
that is Vajrasattva, the truth of the Lotus Family,
who gathers the wisdom of samādhi, the purity of the Lotus Family.
It can purify all sentient beings.
That which is called the "Space Treasury" refers to the great noble wealth that pervades throughout space.
This is the Great Empowerment Dharma; all that belongs to the Ratnasambhava family is an inexhaustible treasury.
The banner of the Great Empowerment Dharma, which skillfully gathers all aspirations, is Vajrasattva himself.
In all maṇḍalas, one should constantly bestow the principle of reality;
the vajra-family empowerment, as well as that of Ratnasaṃbhava and Amitāyus—
the principle of truth is likewise so.
The fundamental insignia are the supreme accomplishment;
through the wondrous principle of reality, they are the sovereign weapons.
The five great secrets are themselves the vajra.
The various insignia of the families are said to be the wisdom of true reality.
Through the supreme conduct of the Buddhas, one realizes great bodhi;
thus, there are the Vajra family, the Ratna family, and the Padma family.
Skillfully gathering all meanings, one accomplishes the secret dharma.
As for the rite of summoning, it refers to the various secret protocols;
using the vajra hook and bell, one performs the summoning.
What is called "all offerings" refers to the various secret rituals;
it means offering with delight through various songs, dances, and so forth.
What is called "the dharma before one's eyes" refers to the various secret rituals.
Each should employ their respective mudrā, and then, with single-minded concentration,
recite the reality-principle.
When all accomplishments appear before one, by means of the Great Samaya rite,
The true and subtle principle is the fundamental emptiness;
it is the nature of Vajrasattva, which is the body of Samantabhadra and also the Lord of Vajra.
As for what is called the "method of accomplishment," it refers to the matters of accomplishment performed within the various ritual manuals;
one should perform all accomplishments in accordance with the dharma of one's chosen deity.
All ritual procedures are accomplished; by holding the bell and vajra according to the Dharma, one awakens the world.
Desiring to achieve all dharmas, one swiftly fulfills the fundamental teaching.
What is called "without toil" means that what is undertaken is accomplished without the need for strenuous application.
Whether following one's desires or obtaining food and drink, even throughout the four modes of deportment, [one remains in meditative concentration].
Whether speaking or engaging in playful laughter, one should simply give rise to a heart of utmost sincerity;
abiding in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) in accordance with the ritual of the *iṣṭadevatā*,
through such principles of union, all dharmas will be swiftly accomplished.
This root Great Teaching is profoundly secret;
if one practices according to the Dharma, all aspirations will be fulfilled.
All the Tathāgatas and all the great Bodhisattvas—
